frameworks.name: Four Types of Leverage
frameworks.definition: A stack of four distinct leverage mechanisms (labor, media, capital, technology) that compound when combined; each type multiplies return on input effort.

frameworks.name: Order of Magnitude Income Transitions
frameworks.definition: Progressive shifts in business structure (employee > self-employed > small team > licensed model > capital deployment) that correspond to $10M+ cumulative income milestones.

claims.text: Leverage is defined as the ratio of output to input: high leverage means you put in a little and get a lot out; low leverage means you put in a lot and get little out. Most people earning below their desired threshold have low-leverage opportunities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi progressed through four distinct orders of magnitude in monthly income by acquiring each type of leverage sequentially: four figures/month (employee), five figures/month (self-employed), six figures/month (hired employees), seven figures/month (licensing model), eight figures/month (capital deployment).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Labor leverage exists in three tiers: first working for someone else, then working for yourself, then hiring others to work for you. Each transition increases output per unit of personal time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each tier removes personal time from the binding constraint.

claims.text: Media leverage (e.g., licensing) involves creating content or intellectual property once and deploying it infinitely across customers without additional production cost, because the cost of goods is essentially zero.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Zero marginal cost enables infinite redeployment without proportional additional input.
bounded_by: Does not apply to physical products with per-unit manufacturing costs
Does not apply to pure service delivery without systematization

claims.text: Capital leverage means deploying money to generate returns without sacrificing personal time; capital has high input-to-output ratio compared to time-based labor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Technology leverage (code-based) theoretically builds a product once and enables a million users to consume it simultaneously, making it the highest-leverage modality after mastery is achieved.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: requires initial product-market fit and user adoption
claims.mechanism: Marginal cost per user approaches zero at scale.
bounded_by: Technology leverage is only captured if users actually adopt the product

claims.text: The quantity of leverage deployed matters as much as the type: Joe Rogan and another podcaster both use media leverage, but Rogan has significantly more of it, resulting in disproportionate returns.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Greater volume multiplies the output-per-input ratio beyond the baseline of the leverage type.

claims.text: Maximum-leverage companies stack all four leverage types simultaneously and maximize the quantity within each: Facebook had other people's money (capital), other people's work (labor), media distribution, and technology infrastructure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Capital sources have tiers with increasing quantities available: friends-and-family funding, institutional money, and public-market capital (e.g., IPO via NASDAQ). Same work applied to a larger capital pool produces proportionally larger returns.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: People who move faster in life do not actually move faster; they get more output per unit of effort by understanding and stacking leverage types.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Leverage efficiency compounds over time, making the appearance of speed a result of force multiplication, not increased pace.

claims.text: A founder's ignorance about hiring alternatives is itself a leverage bottleneck: Hormozi did not realize he could hire people until gym members pointed out he could delegate cleaning, marketing, and teaching.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Belief constraints limit action more than financial constraints in early-stage businesses.

claims.text: Naval Ravikant's model (referenced by Hormozi) identifies four types of leverage: labor, media, capital, and technology, forming a framework for wealth creation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: When Alex Hormozi transitioned from employee to self-employed, he immediately increased his monthly income from four figures to five figures because he captured his own margin instead of paying an employer. This was the moment he realized he could control his own economics. The next transition occurred when gym members suggested he hire them to handle cleaning, marketing, and teaching classes—activities he had been doing himself. That realization led to hiring his first employees and reaching six figures per month.

Hormozi licensed his digital gym product (zero manufacturing cost) and deployed it infinitely to new customers without additional production. This licensing model, operating at essentially zero cost of goods, propelled him from six to seven figures monthly—the jump that proved media leverage was the next multiplicative force after labor leverage.

Hormozi then moved to capital deployment as his eighth-order-of-magnitude shift, deploying capital to generate returns without sacrificing his personal time for delivery or execution. He speculates that nine figures monthly will require either advanced technology or expanded media presence, indicating a continuing pattern of stacking leverage types.

practices.text: Stack as many types of leverage as possible in your business: assess whether you are using labor leverage, media leverage, capital leverage, and technology leverage, then intentionally maximize the quantity of each.

To determine if you have sufficient leverage, measure the gap between input and output; if you are putting in much effort but getting little return, you are operating in a low-leverage opportunity and should pivot toward a higher-leverage model.

When pursuing capital as a leverage lever, investigate the full spectrum of capital sources (friends-and-family, institutional, public markets) to understand how much capital is available to your model; same execution applied to a larger capital pool yields proportionally larger returns.
